newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - T-bond vols bounce back as bonds rally.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - T-bond vols bounce back as bonds rally.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options recouped early losses by midsession as strength in underlying bond prices attracted buying in the short-dated at-the-money calls, traders said.

Volatilities dipped in early trade immediately after the release of June U.S. producer price index data, which showed benign inflationary pressure, as expected, and prompted profit-taking in T-bond futures.
As futures bounced off lows, interest re-emerged in options as well, led by a 3,000-contract purchase in August 114 calls, traders said.

"It (the September futures contract) was right at the 114-handle," said a brokerage firm trader at the Chicago Board of Trade. "We were just breaking above that when they started buying them (114 calls)."
At midsession, September futures were up 16/32 at 114-12/32 after touching a seven-month high of 114-15/32.

"I don't know if there's a huge rush on gamma now, but people buying those at-the-moneys are thinking gamma would work in their favor," the brokerage trader said. He noted that premiums paid for the August 114 calls, which expire next Friday, ranged from about 28/32 to 32/64.

Short-dated at-the-money options have high gamma, which provides quicker premium acceleration, as well as bigger delta swings for delta-neutral volatility traders, although they are vulnerable to time decay.

Implied volatility for August T-bond futures options, which had fallen half a point to about 6.7 percent early on, jumped back to around 7.2 percent. September, which also slipped a few tenths of a point, returned to 8.2 percent.
A couple of 1,000-lot sales of September 114 calls were seen to have led the way in the early volatility selloff that coincided with a pullback in futures after the PPI numbers.
The PPI fell 0.1 percent in June after a 0.3 percent drop in May, roughly in line with the market's forecasts.

Next up prior to the expiration of August options are Tuesday's June retail sales and Wednesday's consumer price index. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony is due on July 22.
In Eurodollars, volatilities were mixed in uneventful trade.

"We saw a little bit of firming up earlier in the week, but maybe it was not so much firming up -- just interest in buying here and there," a bank affiliate trader at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange said.

He saw increased interest in the mid-curves -- options expiring in the coming months but priced off futures in the following year -- in the back months as front-month futures have been relatively subdued.
"I think the expectation is that next week you've got some more interesting data coming out and, of course, Humphrey-Hawkins...always induces some volatility," he added.
Implied volatility for December Eurodollar futures options stood little changed at around 9.3 percent.
